pages: RECOMMENDATION → why is this not a cost problem? Enter on a cluster-plus-catchment node: 94% of a city store's asset productivity, at a site chosen so the break is survivable One node serves a 3–6 college cluster AND its adjacent non-student catchment. The academic calendar enters as a site-selection criterion, not a cost line. 90-day build, one pilot, ₹325 lakh of capital employed. THE MARKET → if we enter, what breaks? Six in ten Indian colleges are rural and metros run 19% over sustainable capacity: a smaller market than it looks, and an emptier one Both facts come out of registers, not forecasts. The first cuts our own addressable universe by 61%. The second is why we still recommend entry. THE SEGMENT HAS ALREADY KILLED AN OPERATOR    Jun 2026: Starship Technologies exited ALL US higher education after 8 years and 60+ campuses, withdrawing ~1,200 robots¹⁵. CEO Ahti Heinla:  “campus and grocery are fundamentally different operations: one is seasonal and contract-driven, the other is a 365-day urban business.”  It lost 365-day utilisation to 8.5-month utilisation — the ratio on slide 4. The campuses did not go dark: Avride took them on a national foodservice master agreement. A contract shape failed, not the segment. THE UNIVERSE NARROWS   ·   AISHE REGISTER, 28-8-2026 54,014 colleges → 21,000 urban (39.4%) → 17,805 urban and non-metro, of which 1,897 are urban high-propensity standalones. Register count [6], not the 2023-24 report count [7]; the two instruments are never mixed. THE DENSIFICATION WALL   ·   ONE QUARTER OF ADDITIONS 900 stores bought 152 new pin codes — 5.9 per pin code, so nine in ten went where an operator already served. Of 6,693 stores across five operators, only 2,393 sit outside the metros. Store density per urban college: metro 1.35 against non-metro 0.13 — 10.0× headroom where the archetype actually sits. AND THE SEGMENT IS UNCOUNTED    Euromonitor's Indian consumer-foodservice taxonomy has no education or institutional location type, and its household typology has no hostel, PG or shared-student category — students fall into “Other”, never broken out¹⁴. This micro-market is not small in the standard dataset; it is absent from it.  We shrink our own market on slide two and still recommend entry.  The question is not whether — it is where, and at what return. Sources 5,6,7,14,15  ·  full screen A7  ·  register vs report note A2

THE RETURN → so which sites supply the density? Density buys back the calendar: 6.93× against a city store's 7.34× — and the node clears the 40% ROCE the client manages to Asset turn is the turnover leg of ROCE. The campus node clears that leg at 94% of a city store; the margin leg is what the basket lever has to buy. Two legs, one identity, in the client's own metric. SITE SELECTION → can we operate inside a gate? The calendar becomes a filter: 569 orders/day of uncontested adjacent demand, 111 districts of 760 — and we disqualified 72% of our own list The filter binds on access revocation (513/day), not on break-period solvency (471/day), so it is set at the higher of the two. A node that survives losing the campus survives the break by construction.  THE FILTER D_adj ≥ max(D_solvency, D_revocation) / (1−κ) κ = contested share of the adjacent catchment   κ=0%   → 569/day      κ=25% → 758/day   κ=10%  → 632/day      κ=44% → 1,015/day  7-WEEK RULE, derived:  21d + 28d = 49d Only the METRO five-operator overlap (44%) is published⁵, so the requirement is a band and we quote the band. Wind-down (T−21d) and ramp-up (28d) collide below 7 weeks, so a shorter break segment cannot be wound down at all. THE SCREEN, AND THEN OUR OWN LIST 760 → 111 on four criteria, then screened for incumbent presence: 9 uncontested, 22 contested, 80 stacked. WHAT THIS FLAG CANNOT DO    Expected incumbent stores = urban colleges × non-metro store density, so ‘uncontested’ is arithmetically ‘6–7 urban colleges’: the 9 clean districts are the 9 smallest, sitting on the screen's own floor. The flag ranks; it does not site. Contestedness and cluster density trade off directly — there is no large empty district, and the plan does not need one:  campus demand inside the gate is uncontested by construction, and what this screen prices is the adjacent half. The register also carries no enrolment⁶, so district student counts are imputed off state ratios⁷ and labelled as such. THE OPERATING MODEL → does the money work? Split the trip at the gate and buy the batch with time: last mile falls ₹42 → ₹19.0 per order, and the product is fastest at exam-night peak Two decisions, one page: the fleet is a labour class, not a vehicle; and the SLA is a batching rule, not a promise. Both are what make the ₹19.0 on slide 3 real. Second lever, unused in the base case: Minutes' free-delivery threshold is ₹149, the market's lowest (Instamart ₹199, Blinkit ₹499, and Blinkit already varies it by location and demand) — an existing platform lever, not a new ask.   ·   NPV at 12% / 15% [assumed; no WACC is disclosed]: ₹158 L / ₹129 L. ROADMAP, RISK, GATE → decision 90 days to a measured go/no-go: four workstreams, four instrumented metrics, and one dependency that can stop the rollout Every action fires on a calendar date, not on observed volume — semester demand steps rather than ramps. The gate metrics are Round 1's metric architecture, now doing the job it was designed for. THE 90 DAYS   ·   WORKSTREAM × WEEK, WITH OWNERS SITE & LICENCE Contracts W1–2 shortlist 6 sites in 2 districts, uncontested-catchment test W3–5 campus licence + DORMANCY CLAUSE in supplier terms W6 sign; publish the academic calendar into the ops calendar  NODE BUILD Cluster ops W3–6 fit-out 2,000 sqft small-format, one chilled zone W7–9 hire 25 store staff; 4-week lead on the rehire pool  FLEET & PARTNER Fleet W5–8 institution runner agreement, per-parcel fee, SLA-linked W8–10 e-cart circuits mapped, OTP chain of custody live  COMMERCIAL Category W6–9 non-grocery mix to 25%: durables, accessories, print, BPC, OTC W10–12 campus free-delivery threshold test vs the ₹149 network floor  Ramp-up cannot be gradual: semester-start demand STEPS, so every ramp action is dated off the published academic calendar. DAY-90 GATE   ·   ROUND 1's METRICS, INSTRUMENTED GATE METRIC THRESHOLD  Peak-to-Trough Demand Ratio > 4.0× Gate-Drop Consolidation Ratio ≥ 3.0×  Term-Weighted CM + Break Runway ≥ 1.0× Calendar-Linked Labour Share ≥ 50% Volume is the first read: at 1,000 orders/day the asset-turn ratio is 0.67 and at −30% the node does not pay back within its life. Measure it before capital goes to node two. THE THREE CONCESSIONS, MADE FROM THE FRONT FOOT    11 minutes is a marketing number (slide 6). The industry relocates rather than mothballs — and we never proposed mothballing; holding costs 24% of one move. We are not first: Swiggy, Blinkit and Zepto are all in the segment (slide 1). None of the three underwrites the node on the cluster. Approve one pilot node, ₹325 lakh of capital employed, and a day-90 gate on four metrics.  If volume clears, node two is a site-selection decision we have already made 111 times.
